title: Judgment at Ichigaya: The Tokyo Trial
subtitle: International Military Tribunal for the Far East, Tokyo, 1946–1948
intro: On 3 May 1946, eight months after the surrender, twenty-eight former leaders of Japan were brought into the auditorium of the old Army Ministry on Ichigaya Heights in Tokyo, refitted with floodlights, interpreters' booths and a long bench for eleven judges from eleven nations. The International Military Tribunal for the Far East had been created on 19 January 1946 by an order of General MacArthur, and it would sit until 12 November 1948. Seven of the accused were hanged at Sugamo Prison in the first hour of 23 December 1948.

The honest record of this trial is mostly not diaries. It is the court's own transcript, exhibits and judgment; the telegrams and statements of the occupying power; the affidavits and testimony of the accused; and the separate opinions of judges who could not agree. Two dated private diaries stand beside them: the Chinese judge Mei Ruao's notes from his hotel room in the spring of 1946, and the diplomat Shigemitsu Mamoru's prison diary from Sugamo. A third diary, Kido Kōichi's daily record of court politics from 1930 to 1945, entered the trial as the prosecution's key exhibit.

The eyes are chosen to give the prosecution, the defence and the bench equal weight. Keenan presented the accused as planners of aggressive war; Kiyose and the American counsel Blakeney argued that the charges were law made after the fact, and set Hiroshima beside Pearl Harbor. Tōjō defended the war as self-defence while shielding the Emperor. On the last day the court split five ways: a majority that convicted all twenty-five survivors, Pal of India who would have acquitted them all, Röling of the Netherlands who dissented in both directions, Bernard of France who objected to how the judgment was reached, and Jaranilla of the Philippines, a survivor of Bataan, who thought the sentences too light. This chapter reports those positions and adds no verdict of its own.

One absence shapes everything: the Emperor. MacArthur's January 1946 telegram advising against an indictment, Keenan's cross-examination of Tōjō in January 1948, Bernard's dissent and Webb's separate opinion all circle the man who was never charged. The evidence of atrocity, from Nanjing to the prisoner-of-war camps, is reported here as the court recorded it, with its scale and the witnesses' names, and without detail.

Copyright limits what can be quoted. Short phrases appear only from US-government publications such as Foreign Relations of the United States; the transcript, the judgment, the opinions and all diaries and memoirs are given as digests in plain words. Where a date comes from standard accounts rather than a document seen, the entry is marked approximate.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. Japanese documents of the period date by the era of the Shōwa Emperor (Hirohito), whose first year was 1926: Shōwa 20 = 1945, Shōwa 21 = 1946, Shōwa 22 = 1947, Shōwa 23 = 1948 and Shōwa 25 = 1950. The indictment was lodged on 29 April 1946 (Shōwa 21), the Emperor's birthday, and the executions took place on 23 December 1948 (Shōwa 23), the birthday of the Crown Prince. Tokyo is fourteen hours ahead of Washington, so a decision dated 20 December in Washington reached Tokyo on the 21st.

eyes.name: International Military Tribunal for the Far East (the court's own record)
eyes.role: Eleven-judge Allied court, presided over by Sir William Webb of Australia; its record is the stenographic transcript, the exhibits and the majority judgment
eyes.side: the court: Australia, Canada, China, France, India, the Netherlands, New Zealand, the Philippines, the UK, the US and the USSR
eyes.where: Former Imperial Army Ministry auditorium, Ichigaya Heights, Tokyo
eyes.language: English and Japanese (simultaneous interpretation; English the record language)
eyes.authenticity: The transcript of proceedings runs to some 48,000 pages; the majority judgment, read in court 4–12 November 1948, to 1,781 pages. Copies are held at the University of Virginia Law Library and elsewhere; Pritchard and Zaide published the transcripts in 22 volumes (1981). All entries here are digests.
eyes.bio: The Tokyo court was created by an order of the Supreme Commander, not by a treaty among governments, and sat for two and a half years. Webb ran it firmly and was later called a dictator by a colleague. Its majority judgment was written by a group of seven judges; five others filed separate opinions. It heard 419 witnesses and took 779 affidavits and depositions.

sources.title: University of Virginia Law Library, IMTFE Digital Collection
Transcript catalogue entry, 3 May 1946 (Morgan Papers)
Peace Palace Library research guide: Tokyo Trial (editions of record)

eyes.name: General Douglas MacArthur (SCAP)
eyes.role: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers in Japan, aged 66–68
eyes.where: GHQ, Dai-Ichi Seimei Building, Hibiya, Tokyo
eyes.authenticity: His telegrams and the 24 November 1948 review statement survive in US government records and are printed in Foreign Relations of the United States (1946 vol. VIII; 1948 vol. VI). US-government publications: short quotations allowed.
eyes.bio: MacArthur proclaimed the tribunal, appointed its judges from nations' nominees, and had the last word on sentences. He also shaped what the court did not do: his January 1946 telegram argued against indicting the Emperor. He watched none of the sessions.

sources.title: FRUS 1946, vol. VIII, doc. 308: MacArthur to Eisenhower, 25 Jan 1946
FRUS 1948, vol. VI, doc. 614: review of sentences, 24 Nov 1948

eyes.name: Joseph Berry Keenan
eyes.role: Chief of Counsel, International Prosecution Section; former US Assistant Attorney General, appointed by President Truman; aged 57–60
eyes.side: prosecution (United States, leading prosecutors from ten other nations)
eyes.where: Tokyo: IPS offices and the Ichigaya courtroom
eyes.form: opening statement, cross-examination (court record), press statements
eyes.authenticity: His opening statement of 4 June 1946 was printed by the US Department of State (Publication 2613, Far Eastern Series 12, 1946), with the Charter and Indictment. His court questions survive in the transcript. Later book: Keenan and Brown, Crimes Against International Law (1950).
eyes.bio: Unlike Nuremberg, Tokyo had a single chief prosecutor, and the post went to an American political lawyer from Ohio and the Justice Department. Allied colleagues complained of his long absences. His most consequential day in court was a cross-examination meant to keep the Emperor clear of blame.

sources.title: Trial of Japanese War Criminals (Dept. of State Publication 2613, GPO 1946) — catalogue
Prosecution Opening Statement, 4 June 1946 (UVA catalogue)

eyes.name: Mei Ruao (Mei Ju-ao)
eyes.role: Judge for the Republic of China; Stanford and University of Chicago trained lawyer, aged 41–44
eyes.where: Imperial Hotel, Tokyo (room 288), and the Ichigaya bench
eyes.authenticity: His Tokyo diary of spring 1946 was published by his family in Chinese and in English as The Tokyo Trial Diaries of Mei Ju-ao (Shanghai Jiao Tong University Press, 2019). It covers the court's founding weeks; it does not run to the judgment. His accounts of later disputes come mostly from writings of the 1950s–60s.
eyes.bio: Mei arrived among the first judges and wrote at night in his hotel room about bombed Tokyo, isolation from home and his reading on war-crimes law. He fought for China's place on the bench and later pressed for a judgment that gave full weight to China's losses. He is the only judge here who kept a dated private diary during the trial.

sources.title: The Tokyo Trial Diaries of Mei Ju-ao (SJTU Press, 2019)
Aisixiang essay on Mei Ruao and the seating dispute (Chinese)

eyes.name: Radhabinod Pal
eyes.role: Judge for India; Calcutta High Court judge and international lawyer, aged 60–62; the last judge appointed
eyes.side: India (appointed while India was still under British rule)
eyes.where: Tokyo bench; his opinion written in Tokyo
eyes.authenticity: His 1,235-page dissent was filed with the record on 12 November 1948 but not read aloud. It was published separately in Calcutta (1953) and was circulated in Japan from 1952. Modern copyright: digest only.
eyes.bio: Pal joined after India protested its absence from the bench. He alone voted to acquit every defendant on every count, holding that crimes against peace were not law before 1945. He did not deny the atrocities; he argued they belonged to other courts. His opinion was later taken up by Japanese nationalists, a use his admirers and critics still argue over.

sources.title: Separate opinions of the justices (Northcroft Collection, University of Canterbury)
National WWII Museum: Justice Radhabinod Pal and the Tokyo Tribunal

eyes.name: Bernard Victor Aloysius Röling
eyes.role: Judge for the Netherlands, aged 39–42; later professor of international law at Groningen
eyes.authenticity: His 249-page opinion is in the court record and in Röling and Rüter, The Tokyo Judgment (1977). His reflections, The Tokyo Trial and Beyond (with Antonio Cassese, Polity, 1993), were published after his death and are flagged as later.
eyes.bio: The youngest judge, Röling arrived expecting to follow Nuremberg and came to doubt the aggressive-war charges, while holding that conventional war crimes deserved punishment. He dissented in both directions: some defendants he would have acquitted, others he would have punished more severely. He and Pal became friends.

sources.title: Separate opinions of the justices (University of Canterbury)
Peace Palace Library guide (The Tokyo Trial and Beyond)

eyes.name: Henri Bernard
eyes.role: Judge for France; colonial magistrate and Free French officer, aged 47–49
eyes.authenticity: His 23-page dissent is part of the official record of separate opinions, 12 November 1948. Digest only.
eyes.bio: Bernard objected to how the judgment was reached as much as to what it said: the judges had never met as a full bench to debate it. He named the Emperor as a principal whose absence weakened the whole case. His is the shortest of the dissents.

sources.title: Separate opinions of the justices (University of Canterbury)
Famous Trials: Judges of the IMTFE

eyes.name: Delfín Jaranilla
eyes.role: Judge for the Philippines; former Attorney General and survivor of the Bataan death march, aged 62–65
eyes.vantage_label: concurring judge (and former prisoner of war)
eyes.authenticity: His 35-page concurring opinion is in the official record, 12 November 1948. The defence had objected to his sitting because he had been a prisoner of the Japanese army. Digest only.
eyes.bio: Jaranilla was the only judge who had himself been a captive of the forces on trial. He agreed with the convictions and thought several sentences too light. He answered the defence's atomic-bomb arguments directly in his opinion.

sources.title: Separate opinions of the justices (University of Canterbury)
Famous Trials: Judges of the IMTFE

eyes.name: Tōjō Hideki
eyes.role: General; Prime Minister of Japan October 1941–July 1944; defendant, aged 61–64
eyes.where: Sugamo Prison and the defendants' dock at Ichigaya
eyes.authenticity: His long affidavit (defence document read 26 December 1947) and cross-examination are in the transcript. Prison writings and poems were published later by family and associates; they are not used here.
eyes.bio: Arrested after a failed suicide attempt in September 1945, Tōjō became the face of the trial for Allied publics. In the witness box he defended Japan's war as self-defence and took responsibility for it as head of government, while working to keep the Emperor clear. He was hanged with six others.

sources.title: Affidavit of Tōjō, exhibit 3655, 26 Dec 1947 (Georgetown Law Library)
IMTFE proceedings, 26 December 1947 (UNM)

eyes.name: Marquis Kido Kōichi
eyes.role: Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal 1940–1945, closest political adviser to the Emperor; defendant, aged 56–59
eyes.vantage_label: the accused whose diary became the prosecution's key exhibit
eyes.form: diary (prewar diary entered as evidence; interrogations and testimony)
eyes.authenticity: Kido's diary of 1930–1945 was surrendered to the prosecution after his detention and became its principal documentary source; it was later published as Kido Kōichi nikki (University of Tokyo Press, 1966), with a trial-period volume in 1980. Digest only.
eyes.bio: Kido had written up the court's inner politics day by day for fifteen years. Handed over partly to show the Emperor's caution, the diary also supplied the prosecution with the meetings and names it needed against others, and against Kido himself. He was sentenced to life and paroled in 1955.

sources.title: Gendai Business: Kido's diary and his Sugamo interrogations (Japanese)
Hirota v. MacArthur, 338 U.S. 197 (Kido et al. v. MacArthur)

eyes.name: Shigemitsu Mamoru
eyes.role: Diplomat; Foreign Minister 1943–45 and signer of the surrender on the USS Missouri; defendant, aged 58–61
eyes.vantage_label: the accused, keeping a prison diary
eyes.authenticity: His prison diary was published as Sugamo nikki (Bungei Shunjū Shinsha, 1953; continuation volume 1953) and reissued in modern script (Heart Publishing, 2023). Exact daily entries are not confirmed here; entries using it are marked approx.
eyes.bio: Shigemitsu, who had lost a leg to a bomb in Shanghai in 1932, was added to the defendants late at Soviet insistence. His diary looks at the trial from the cell block: fellow prisoners, rumours, the slow sessions. He received the lightest sentence, seven years, was paroled in 1950 and became Foreign Minister again in 1954.

sources.title: Sugamo nikki, continuation volume (1953), NDL record
Sugamo nikki, modern-script edition (2023), NDL record

eyes.name: Kiyose Ichirō
eyes.role: Lawyer and politician; deputy chief of the Japanese defence counsel and Tōjō's principal counsel, aged 61–64
eyes.authenticity: His general opening statement for the defence is in the transcript; parts were ruled out by the bench. His later book Hiroku Tōkyō saiban (1967) is a memoir and is not used for dated entries.
eyes.bio: Kiyose argued that the Charter applied law after the fact and that Japan had fought in self-defence. A veteran parliamentarian, he later served as Speaker of the House of Representatives. He represents the Japanese bar's case, distinct from the American counsel's.

sources.title: UVA IMTFE Digital Collection (defence opening, 1947)

eyes.name: Ben Bruce Blakeney
eyes.role: US Army major and lawyer assigned to the defence; counsel for Tōgō Shigenori and Umezu Yoshijirō, aged 37–40
eyes.authenticity: His arguments and cross-examinations are in the transcript. Some of his May 1946 argument on the atomic bomb is reported not to have been interpreted into Japanese at the time; that detail is not confirmed here.
eyes.bio: Blakeney took the defence of former enemies seriously enough to attack the court's foundations. In May 1946 he set Pearl Harbor beside Hiroshima to argue that killing in war was not murder under international law. He stayed in Japan, lectured in law at Tokyo University and helped translate Tōgō's memoir.

sources.title: Ben Bruce Blakeney (biography summary)

eyes.name: Aisin-Gioro Puyi (Henry Pu-yi)
eyes.role: Last Qing emperor; head of state of Manchukuo 1932–1945; Soviet prisoner brought to Tokyo as prosecution witness, aged 40
eyes.authenticity: His testimony is in the transcript for mid-to-late August 1946. His autobiography, The First Half of My Life (1964), written in Chinese custody and revised under supervision, says he concealed his own role in Tokyo; it is a later and partly directed text.
eyes.bio: Puyi spent the longest time of any witness on the stand, describing himself as a captive of the Kwantung Army. Defence counsel worked to show he had cooperated willingly. His later memoir partly concedes their point, which makes him one of the few eyes here who revised his own testimony in print.

sources.title: Trial transcript, 16 August 1946 (Magee; Henry Pu-Yi), UVA
IMTFE proceedings, 27 August 1946 (UNM)

entries.headline: The diary notes a minister refusing to resign
entries.digest: Kido records that Kishi Nobusuke, a minister of state in the Tōjō cabinet, came to consult him after Tōjō demanded his resignation, and that Kishi refused. The Tōjō cabinet fell the next day. Entries like this, written for no court, later let prosecutors reconstruct who met whom and when.
entries.source_note: Kido diary, 17 July 1944, as cited in Gendai Business article on Kido's interrogations: https://gendai.media/articles/-/49842

entries.headline: A single American prosecutor arrives to build the case
entries.digest: Keenan, appointed by President Truman, arrives in occupied Tokyo with American staff to set up the International Prosecution Section. Unlike Nuremberg's four co-equal prosecutors, the Allied prosecutors here will serve as associates under him. The defendants have not yet been chosen.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia/Wikiwand 'Tokyo Trial' (appointment by Truman); arrival month from standard accounts: https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Tokyo_Trial

entries.headline: The Emperor's adviser enters Sugamo
entries.digest: Kido reports to Sugamo Prison as a war-crimes suspect. Over the next three months he is interrogated about thirty times, and his diary becomes the prosecution's main documentary source on the inner politics of 1930–1945.
entries.source_note: Gendai Business: detained 16 Dec 1945; questioned 30 times in three months: https://gendai.media/articles/-/49842

entries.headline: A proclamation creates the court
entries.digest: MacArthur issues a special proclamation establishing the International Military Tribunal for the Far East and approves its Charter the same day. The Charter follows the Nuremberg model, listing crimes against peace, conventional war crimes and crimes against humanity. The court is a creature of the Supreme Commander, not of a treaty.
entries.source_note: Wikiwand 'Tokyo Trial'; Encyclopedia.com 'Tokyo Trial'; National WWII Museum: https://www.nationalww2museum.org/node/54678

entries.headline: MacArthur advises Washington against indicting the Emperor
entries.digest: In a telegram to Army Chief of Staff Eisenhower, MacArthur reports that his staff has found no specific evidence tying the Emperor to political decisions. He warns that an indictment would provoke upheaval requiring a vast occupation force for years. He leaves the decision to higher policy but makes his own view plain.
entries.source_note: FRUS 1946 vol. VIII, doc. 308 (US government record): https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1946v08/d308

entries.headline: His own diary read back to him
entries.digest: At his twentieth interrogation, investigators use a 1941 diary entry recording a dinner with Kishi Nobusuke to establish Kishi's place in the wartime cabinet. Kido's careful daily notes become the scaffolding on which suspects other than Kido are identified and questioned.
entries.source_note: Gendai Business, citing Kido's 20th interrogation and diary entry of 26 Feb 1941: https://gendai.media/articles/-/49842

entries.place: Atsugi airfield and the Imperial Hotel, Tokyo
entries.headline: Arrival over a burned city
entries.digest: Mei flies in from Shanghai, lands at Atsugi in the afternoon and is driven to the Imperial Hotel. The American officer who meets him gets his name wrong. On the road he notes the bomb-flattened stretches of Yokohama and Tokyo, the first sight of the enemy capital for a judge from a country invaded for eight years.
entries.source_note: Tokyo Trial Diaries of Mei Ju-ao, entry for 20 March 1946 (SJTU Press, 2019): https://www.perlego.com/es/book/3483237/the-tokyo-trial-diaries-of-mei-juao-pdf

entries.headline: Reading war-crimes law in a hotel room
entries.digest: Mei spends the day indoors reading Sheldon Glueck's study of how war criminals might be prosecuted, and watches Japanese pedestrians and American soldiers in the street below. The day before, he had complained that six months into the occupation there was still no official mail route home to China.
entries.source_note: Tokyo Trial Diaries of Mei Ju-ao, entries 21–22 March 1946: https://www.perlego.com/es/book/3483237/the-tokyo-trial-diaries-of-mei-juao-pdf

entries.headline: Twenty-eight men indicted on the Emperor's birthday
entries.digest: At a brief preliminary hearing the prosecution lodges its indictment against 28 former leaders: generals, admirals, prime ministers, diplomats and a propagandist. The counts run from a conspiracy to wage aggressive war dating from 1928 to murder and conventional war crimes. The Emperor is not among them.
entries.source_note: Encyclopedia.com 'Tokyo Trial' (indictment lodged 29 Apr 1946); Famous Trials chronology: https://famous-trials.com/tokyo-war-crimes-trial/2732-tokyo-war-crimes-trial-chronology

entries.headline: The chief prosecutor speaks to the press
entries.digest: Keenan issues a press statement with the indictment, presenting the case as a prosecution of the leaders who planned the war rather than of the Japanese people. The text of the Charter, the indictment and his later opening statement were printed together by the US Department of State in 1946.
entries.source_note: Wikiwand 'Tokyo Trial' (press statement with indictment); State Dept Publication 2613: https://libcat.library.tamu.edu/Record/in00001389228

entries.headline: A late addition to the dock
entries.digest: Shigemitsu, the diplomat who had signed the surrender aboard the USS Missouri, is taken into custody and added to the defendants, together with General Umezu, after the Soviet prosecutor pressed for them. In Sugamo he begins the diary later published as Sugamo nikki.
entries.source_note: Arrest date per standard accounts; diary: Sugamo nikki (1953), NDL: https://ndlsearch.ndl.go.jp/en/books/R100000002-I000000914743

entries.headline: A rehearsal and a quarrel over seats
entries.digest: At the dress rehearsal the day before the opening, a dispute over the order of the judges' seats comes to a head. Mei refuses to take part unless the bench is ordered by the sequence of the surrender signatures, which would put China beside the United States. The president gives way to a vote, and Mei takes a seat beside him.
entries.source_note: Aisixiang essay on Mei Ruao (dispute peaks at the 2 May rehearsal); account derives mainly from Mei's later writings: https://www.aisixiang.com/data/63757.html

entries.headline: The court opens in the old Army Ministry
entries.digest: The tribunal convenes at 11:22 in the auditorium of the former Army Ministry, rebuilt with floodlights for film cameras. Webb opens and the clerks begin reading the indictment. Later in the session the defendant Ōkawa Shūmei, behaving erratically, strikes Tōjō on the head from behind and is removed; he is later found unfit to stand trial.
entries.source_note: Transcript catalogue, 3 May 1946 (convened 11:22, adjourned 16:40): https://imtfe.law.virginia.edu/node/31445; Encyclopedia.com on Ōkawa's disruption: https://www.encyclopedia.com/law/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/tokyo-trial

entries.headline: Pearl Harbor set beside Hiroshima
entries.digest: Arguing defence motions against the court's jurisdiction, Blakeney contends that killing in war is not murder under international law and that waging war is not an individual crime. He sets the death of an American admiral at Pearl Harbor beside the bombing of Hiroshima and asks whether the court would call both murder. The bench reserves its ruling.
entries.source_note: Blakeney biography summary (May 1946 argument): https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Ben_Bruce_Blakeney; exact day per standard accounts

entries.headline: Challenges to jurisdiction rejected, reasons later
entries.digest: The tribunal dismisses the defence motions challenging its jurisdiction and the legality of the Charter, saying its reasons will be given later. They are delivered only in the final judgment two and a half years on. The court sets the start of the prosecution's evidence for early June.
entries.source_note: Famous Trials chronology (17 May 1946): https://famous-trials.com/tokyo-war-crimes-trial/2732-tokyo-war-crimes-trial-chronology

entries.headline: The prosecution opens its case
entries.digest: Keenan delivers the prosecution's opening statement, running to about a hundred pages of transcript. He frames the case as a defence of civilisation against aggressive war and individual leaders' responsibility for it. The State Department printed the speech in Washington that year.
entries.source_note: Prosecution Opening Statement, 4 June 1946 (UVA, transcript pp. 381–489): https://imtfe.law.virginia.edu/node/33739; Dept. of State Publication 2613

entries.headline: Nanjing witnesses take the stand
entries.digest: In the China phase, Western residents who stayed in Nanjing in 1937–38 testify, among them the surgeon Robert Wilson, who describes his hospital filled beyond capacity for weeks from 13 December 1937. The American missionary John Magee follows in August. The court hears this evidence without cross-examination of great length.
entries.source_note: History Room summary of Wilson's testimony: https://history-room.co.uk/2021/03/09/imtfe-tokyo/; Magee listed in transcript of 16 Aug 1946: https://imtfe.law.virginia.edu/node/12034

entries.headline: Testing the puppet story
entries.digest: In cross-examination Blakeney and other defence counsel press Puyi on whether he had cooperated willingly, putting to him a letter in his name to a Japanese general. Puyi calls the letter a forgery and holds to his account. The exchanges are among the most combative of the trial.
entries.source_note: Proceedings for 27 Aug 1946 (UNM): https://nmarchives.unm.edu/repositories/22/archival_objects/179991; details per standard accounts

entries.headline: The last emperor of China in the witness box
entries.digest: Puyi, flown in from Soviet custody, begins one of the longest testimonies of the trial. He describes himself as a puppet held under Japanese military control in Manchukuo, unable to refuse. The same day's transcript also records the end of John Magee's Nanjing evidence.
entries.source_note: Trial transcript 16 Aug 1946, pp. 4566–4656, witnesses Magee and Henry Pu-Yi (Sutton Papers): https://imtfe.law.virginia.edu/node/12034

entries.headline: The prosecution rests
entries.digest: After 192 court days and evidence in fifteen phases, from Manchuria to the treatment of prisoners of war, the prosecution closes its case-in-chief. Defence motions to dismiss follow and are rejected.
entries.source_note: Wikiwand 'Tokyo Trial'; Encyclopedia.com 'Tokyo Trial'

entries.headline: The defence states Japan's case
entries.digest: Kiyose delivers the general opening statement for the defence. He argues that the Charter created crimes after the fact, that Japan acted in self-defence against encirclement and communism, and that the Emperor's government had sought peace. The bench rules parts of the statement irrelevant and has them struck.
entries.source_note: Papers Past headline 'Defence counsel opens case for the Jap war leaders', 25 Feb 1947 (site blocked at fetch); standard accounts

entries.headline: The diarist testifies for himself
entries.digest: Kido takes the stand in his own defence and explains his diary as the record of a court official working for restraint. Cross-examination turns the same pages against him and against the army leaders he had named. Other defendants resent how much his notes have given the prosecution.
entries.source_note: Month per standard accounts; NDL record of a 1940s pamphlet on 'Kido testimony at the Tokyo Trial'

entries.headline: Tōjō's affidavit is read
entries.digest: Defence counsel read Tōjō's long affidavit into the record. It defends Japan's decisions of 1941 as forced by economic blockade and American demands, accepts responsibility as head of government, and denies that the Emperor bore blame. It is entered as exhibit 3655.
entries.source_note: Affidavit of Tōjō, exhibit 3655, 26 Dec 1947 (Georgetown): https://aspace.ll.georgetown.edu/public/repositories/3/archival_objects/10073; UNM proceedings 26 Dec 1947

entries.headline: A slip about the Emperor's will
entries.digest: Questioned by counsel for Kido, Tōjō says no Japanese subject would have acted against the Emperor's will. The answer implies the Emperor had approved the war. The prosecution, committed to keeping the Emperor out of the case, moves to have the point revisited.
entries.source_note: Standard accounts of the cross-examination; date not confirmed from the transcript here

entries.headline: Cross-examination steers away from the throne
entries.digest: Keenan's questions lead Tōjō to say that the Emperor had wanted peace up to the outbreak of war and throughout it, and that going to war may have been against his wishes. Tōjō also says he did not brief the Emperor on Pearl Harbor during audiences in the first week of December 1941.
entries.source_note: Levin Chronicle, 7 Jan 1948, p. 5, dateline Tokyo 6 Jan: https://dynamic-rsnz.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/CHRONL19480107.2.30

entries.headline: Tōjō restates: the Emperor had wanted peace
entries.digest: Under Keenan's questioning Tōjō revises the impression he had left: the Emperor consented to war reluctantly, on his ministers' advice. The correction is widely reported abroad. It aligns the defendant and the prosecutor on one point both wanted settled.
entries.source_note: Levin Chronicle, 7 Jan 1948: https://dynamic-rsnz.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/CHRONL19480107.2.30; Georgetown: cross-examination of Tōjō, 3 Jan 1948: https://aspace.ll.georgetown.edu/public/repositories/3/archival_objects/14135

entries.headline: Leaving the witness box
entries.digest: Tōjō ends his testimony saying he believed he had acted rightly for his country. He returns to the dock for the remaining months of rebuttal and summations.
entries.source_note: Famous Trials chronology (7 Jan 1948): https://famous-trials.com/tokyo-war-crimes-trial/2732-tokyo-war-crimes-trial-chronology

entries.headline: The court withdraws to write
entries.digest: After two months of summations the tribunal adjourns to deliberate. The majority of seven begins drafting a judgment that will take seven months; the dissenting judges write their own opinions separately.
entries.source_note: Encyclopedia.com 'Tokyo Trial'; Famous Trials chronology

entries.headline: Webb begins reading the judgment
entries.digest: Webb begins reading the majority judgment aloud, a task that will take seven court days. It finds that a criminal conspiracy to wage aggressive war existed from 1928 and recounts the evidence on Nanjing, where it estimates more than 200,000 civilians and prisoners were killed in the first weeks, and on the death rates of prisoners of war. The defendants listen through interpreters' headphones.
entries.source_note: Encyclopedia.com and Famous Trials (reading 4–12 Nov 1948); Nanjing figure from judgment ch. VIII per standard accounts

entries.headline: Twenty-five convicted, seven to hang
entries.digest: The defendants are called one by one for sentence. Seven are sentenced to death by hanging: Tōjō, Hirota, Itagaki, Doihara, Matsui, Kimura and Mutō. Sixteen receive life, Tōgō twenty years and Shigemitsu seven. Webb's separate opinion, filed the same day, says the Emperor's immunity should have weighed in the sentences.
entries.source_note: Wikiwand 'Tokyo Trial'; Separate opinions, Northcroft Collection: https://www.canterbury.ac.nz/study/library/search-our-collections/art-and-archives/archives-collection/justice-erima-harvey-northcroft-tokyo-war-crimes-trial-collectio/separate-opinions-of-the-justices

entries.headline: One judge would acquit them all
entries.digest: Pal's dissent, filed but not read in court, would acquit every defendant on every count. He holds that crimes against peace were created after the fact, finds the conspiracy unproved, and sets Japan's conduct beside Western colonial empires. He accepts that atrocities such as those at Nanjing occurred but treats them as matters for other trials, and he condemns the atomic bombings.
entries.source_note: Northcroft Collection (1,235 pp.); National WWII Museum article: https://www.nationalww2museum.org/node/54756

entries.headline: A dissent that cuts both ways
entries.digest: Röling's opinion doubts that aggressive war was an individual crime in law but accepts liability for war crimes, including by omission. He would acquit several defendants, among them the former prime minister Hirota, and finds others deserving heavier punishment than they received.
entries.source_note: Northcroft Collection (249 pp.); Wikiwand 'Tokyo Trial'

entries.headline: The French judge: a flawed procedure
entries.digest: Bernard's dissent says the eleven judges never deliberated together on the judgment, so its verdict cannot stand as the court's. He calls the Emperor a principal author of the war whose absence from the dock left the case unequal.
entries.source_note: Northcroft Collection (23 pp.); Famous Trials: Judges of the IMTFE

entries.headline: The Philippine judge: sentences too light
entries.digest: Jaranilla concurs with the convictions and argues that several penalties are too lenient for the gravity of the crimes. His opinion also takes up the atomic bomb, rejecting the defence's use of it to excuse the accused.
entries.source_note: Northcroft Collection (35 pp.: 'incommensurate penalties', 'the atomic bomb'); Wikiwand 'Tokyo Trial'

entries.headline: Sentenced to death by hanging
entries.digest: Called to the dock, Tōjō hears his sentence through headphones, nods and leaves. He is convicted on counts of conspiracy, waging aggressive war and responsibility for the mistreatment of prisoners of war.
entries.source_note: Wikiwand 'Tokyo Trial'; History.com, 3 May

entries.headline: Life imprisonment for the diarist
entries.digest: Kido is sentenced to imprisonment for life. The diary he surrendered to clear the throne has helped convict him and others. He is paroled in 1955.
entries.source_note: Encyclopedia.com 'Tokyo Trial' (life; paroled 1955)

entries.headline: Seven years, the lightest sentence
entries.digest: Shigemitsu receives seven years, the shortest term handed down. His diary returns from the courtroom to the prison routine and the condemned men's last weeks in the same building.
entries.source_note: Sentence verified (Wikiwand 'Tokyo Trial'); diary content for the day not confirmed: Sugamo nikki (1953)

entries.headline: A judge writes to the Japanese public
entries.digest: On the day of sentence Mei publishes an open letter to the Japanese people in the Asahi Shimbun, urging them to reckon with the war. He had pressed in chambers for a judgment that gave China's losses their full weight and for the Emperor to have been tried.
entries.source_note: Aisixiang essay on Mei Ruao: https://www.aisixiang.com/data/63757.html (letter not seen in the original)

entries.headline: The Supreme Commander confirms every sentence
entries.digest: After consulting the Allied representatives in Tokyo, MacArthur announces that he finds nothing in the proceedings to warrant his intervention and orders the Eighth Army to carry out the sentences. He calls the duty deeply distasteful and asks for prayers for peace.
entries.quote: If we cannot trust such processes and such men
entries.source_note: FRUS 1948 vol. VI, doc. 614 (Sebald to Secretary of State, telegram 273): https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1948v06/d614

entries.place: Washington (case of Kido et al. v. MacArthur)
entries.headline: The US Supreme Court declines to intervene
entries.digest: Petitions for habeas corpus filed for Hirota, Doihara and Kido and others are denied. The Court rules, per curiam, that the Tokyo tribunal was set up by MacArthur as agent of the Allied Powers and is not a United States court, so American courts cannot review it.
entries.source_note: Hirota v. MacArthur, 338 U.S. 197 (argued 16–17 Dec, decided 20 Dec 1948): https://chanrobles.com/usa/us_supremecourt/338/197/case.php

entries.headline: Executions at Sugamo, without cameras
entries.digest: Shortly after midnight the seven condemned men are hanged in Sugamo Prison, with Allied representatives present as witnesses. MacArthur bars photography of the executions. The next day the remaining unindicted Class A suspects are released.
entries.source_note: Wikiwand 'Tokyo Trial'; Famous Trials chronology; History Room (timings): https://history-room.co.uk/2021/03/09/imtfe-tokyo/

entries.headline: Hanged in the first group
entries.digest: Tōjō is hanged in the first group of four, with Doihara, Matsui and Mutō, shortly after midnight; the second group follows within the half hour.
entries.source_note: History Room summary (12:08 a.m.–12:35 a.m.): https://history-room.co.uk/2021/03/09/imtfe-tokyo/; Wikiwand 'Tokyo Trial'

entries.headline: Paroled, and back to politics
entries.digest: Shigemitsu walks out of Sugamo on parole, two years after sentence. He publishes his prison diary in 1953 and becomes Foreign Minister again in 1954.
entries.source_note: Nikkan Gendai photo caption (parole 21 Nov 1950): https://www.nikkan-gendai.com/articles/view/news/383028

entries.headline: The dissent finds a Japanese audience
entries.digest: After the occupation ends in April 1952, Pal's dissent is published and widely read in Japan, and Pal visits the country. His argument that the trial was victors' justice becomes a touchstone for critics of the verdict, a use that historians still debate.
entries.source_note: Standard accounts; Peace Palace Library lists Calcutta edition of 1953: https://peacepalacelibrary.nl/research-guide/tokyo-trial

entries.headline: The witness revises his testimony
entries.digest: In his autobiography, written in Chinese custody and published in 1964, Puyi says he had concealed his own willing cooperation with the Japanese when he testified in Tokyo, to protect himself. The book was written under official supervision and is itself a directed text.
entries.source_note: Puyi, The First Half of My Life (1964), per standard accounts

entries.headline: Looking back on Tokyo
entries.digest: In conversations with Antonio Cassese, published after his death, Röling recalls Webb as domineering and explains his own dissent and his friendship with Pal. These are later reflections, not records of 1946–48.
entries.source_note: Röling and Cassese, The Tokyo Trial and Beyond (Polity, 1993), per Peace Palace Library; Famous Trials judges page

claims.claim: Special proclamation establishes the IMTFE and approves its Charter
claims.evidence: SCAP special proclamation; Charter printed in Dept. of State Publication 2613 (1946)

claims.claim: No specific evidence found tying the Emperor to political decisions; indictment would require a vast occupation force
Indictment lodged against 28 defendants, from conspiracy to aggressive war (from 1928) to conventional war crimes
Killing in war is not murder under international law; Hiroshima set beside Pearl Harbor
Defence challenges to jurisdiction dismissed, reasons reserved to the judgment
Opening statement: the accused leaders personally responsible for planning aggressive war
claims.evidence: Transcript pp. 381–489; Dept. of State Publication 2613

claims.claim: Testifies that he was a puppet ruler under Japanese army control in Manchukuo
Defence opening: Charter law is ex post facto; Japan fought in self-defence
claims.evidence: IMTFE transcript; parts struck by the bench

claims.claim: Affidavit: the 1941 decisions were self-defence; responsibility his as head of government, not the Emperor's
Under Keenan's questioning: the Emperor desired peace and consented to war reluctantly
Majority: conspiracy proved; 25 convicted; seven sentenced to death, sixteen to life, two to terms
claims.evidence: Judgment of the IMTFE (1,781 pp.) and sentences

claims.claim: Dissent: all defendants should be acquitted on all counts; crimes against peace not law before 1945
claims.evidence: Dissentient judgment of the member from India (1,235 pp.)

claims.claim: Dissent: no full-bench deliberation; the Emperor's absence left the case unequal
claims.evidence: Dissenting judgment of the member from France (23 pp.)

claims.claim: Concurrence: several penalties too lenient for the gravity of the offences
claims.evidence: Concurring opinion of the member from the Philippines (35 pp.)

claims.claim: Review: no grounds to intervene; Eighth Army directed to execute the sentences
US Supreme Court: the tribunal is not a US court; habeas petitions denied

convergences.label: Indictment day, the Emperor's birthday
convergences.note: The court records 28 names; the prosecutor presents them as the planners of the war, not the nation; and the diplomat who signed the surrender finds himself among them at the last minute, while the man in whose name the war was fought is absent from the list.

convergences.label: The opening at Ichigaya
convergences.note: Mei's fight the day before was about where China would sit; the court's record of the opening is about procedure and an indictment read aloud. The Ōkawa incident is the moment the cameras remembered.

convergences.label: The court's foundations challenged
convergences.note: An American officer argues for Japanese defendants that the court's charges are not law; three days later the court rejects the motions but defers its reasons until the judgment.

convergences.label: Puyi on the stand
convergences.note: The prosecution's star witness presents himself as a captive; the defence presents him as a willing partner; his own memoir, eighteen years later, partly concedes the defence's point.

convergences.label: The Emperor question in the witness box
convergences.note: Prosecutor and accused, on opposite sides of everything else, reach the same answer on one point: the Emperor wanted peace. Bernard and Mei would later say the Emperor should have been tried.

convergences.label: Sentence day and five separate opinions
convergences.note: The same evidence yields a majority conviction, a call to acquit everyone, a dissent in both directions, a complaint about procedure and a call for harsher penalties, while the defendants hear their sentences one by one.

convergences.label: Last appeals and the executions
convergences.note: Washington's highest court disclaims power over the court MacArthur created; three days later his Eighth Army carries out the sentences, with cameras barred.

ties.note: Keenan cross-examined Tōjō in January 1948, steering his testimony toward the Emperor's wish for peace.
Kiyose was Tōjō's principal Japanese counsel and opened the defence case in February 1947.
Blakeney was among the defence counsel who cross-examined Puyi in August 1946 on whether he had served Japan willingly.
Keenan's prosecution section operated under SCAP, and MacArthur's decision not to pursue the Emperor framed what Keenan would charge.
The two dissenters became friends in Tokyo and shared doubts about the aggressive-war charges, though they reached different verdicts on individual defendants.
Mei pressed for a firm conviction that recognised China's losses; Pal would have acquitted all defendants.
MacArthur argued in January 1946 against indicting the Emperor; Bernard's dissent named the Emperor's absence as a fatal inequality.
Kido's diary recorded his role in bringing Tōjō to power in 1941 and in the cabinet's fall in 1944; the prosecution used it against both.
Both were held in Sugamo Prison through the trial and both were sentenced on 12 November 1948.
On the same day one judge called the sentences too lenient and another called for acquittal of all.
Blakeney raised the atomic bombings in the defendants' favour; Jaranilla's opinion rejected the comparison.
Kido was among the petitioners in Kido et al. v. MacArthur, denied by the US Supreme Court on 20 December 1948.

threads_out.note: The Tokyo Charter of 19 January 1946 copied the London Charter's categories of crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity, and the British judge at Tokyo aimed to uphold the Nuremberg judgment of October 1946. Tokyo differed in having a single American chief prosecutor and a court created by one commander's order.

The men in the Ichigaya dock were the leaders of the war whose last months Volume I follows; Shigemitsu, who signed the surrender on the USS Missouri on 2 September 1945, became a defendant in April 1946, and Blakeney raised Hiroshima in court in May 1946.
Robert Wilson and John Magee, who had stayed in Nanjing in 1937–38, testified at Tokyo in 1946; the majority judgment's findings on Nanjing led in part to General Matsui Iwane's death sentence.
